meta.note: Specific models, priced at anchor years rather than annually. An anchor is a year I have an actual view on; the app draws markers at anchors and interpolates between them, so the interpolation is never mistaken for data. CAGR is computed endpoint-to-endpoint from anchors only.

kinds.retail: Boutique list price. Rising retail is what the object COSTS you, not what you earn — benchmarked against CPI.
kinds.resale: Secondary-market or auction value. This is the investment question — benchmarked against the S&P 500.

items.name: Rolex Daytona
items.blurb: The hype watch of the 2010s. Launched at $12,400 retail and never sold at retail.
items.source: Secondary-market asking prices; the 2021-22 peak and subsequent fall are widely reported
items.caveat: Anyone who actually paid retail did far better than this line — but waitlists meant almost nobody could.

items.name: Rolex Submariner Date
items.blurb: What Rolex charges at the counter.
items.source: Published US list prices
items.caveat: List price, not what you could actually buy one for.

items.name: Rolex Submariner Date
items.blurb: The same watch on the grey market — the gap over list is the whole story.
items.source: Secondary-market asking prices
items.caveat: Grey-market pricing is thin and dealer-quoted; spreads are wide.

items.name: Patek Philippe Nautilus
items.blurb: The most extreme watch bubble on record. Retail was about $34,900 when Patek discontinued it in 2021.
items.source: Secondary-market asking prices
items.caveat: The single best illustration of why the start year decides everything. Buy in 2021, lose half.

items.name: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak
items.blurb: The third of the steel-sports-watch trinity.
items.source: Secondary-market asking prices
items.caveat: Reference changed mid-series (15400 to 15500 in 2019); treated as one continuous model line.

items.name: Omega Speedmaster Professional
items.blurb: The sane man's grail. Actually available at retail, which is why it never bubbled.
items.source: Published US list prices
items.caveat: The 2021 jump reflects the new co-axial master chronometer movement — not quite like-for-like.

items.name: Hermès Birkin 30
items.blurb: The boutique price — if Hermès will sell you one, which is the catch.
items.source: Reported US retail prices
items.caveat: Hermès does not publish a price list; these are widely-reported figures. Leather and hardware change the price substantially.

items.name: Hermès Birkin 30
items.blurb: The rare object that reliably resells above what the shop charged.
items.source: Resale-platform asking prices
items.caveat: Condition, colour and hardware swing this enormously; a neutral-colour example in excellent condition is assumed.

items.name: Chanel Classic Flap
items.blurb: The most aggressive price escalation in luxury retail. Chanel raised this bag roughly sevenfold in twenty years.
items.source: Widely-reported US retail prices across repeated increases
items.caveat: The headline number of this whole project: as a COST this outran inflation about fourfold. It is only a return if you owned one and sold it.

items.name: Louis Vuitton Neverfull MM
items.blurb: The entry-level status bag, and a clean read on mass-luxury price inflation.
items.source: Published US retail prices
items.caveat: Coated canvas, not leather — it does not hold resale value the way the Hermès and Chanel entries do.

items.name: Ferrari F40
items.blurb: The poster car, and one of the best-performing physical assets of the last fifteen years.
items.source: Auction results and market guides
items.caveat: Excludes maintenance, which on an F40 is not a rounding error — engine-out services run five figures.

items.name: Ferrari Testarossa
items.blurb: Worth less in 2010 than in 2005, then tripled.
items.source: Auction results and market guides
items.caveat: A reminder that classic cars can sit flat or fall for a decade at a time.

items.name: Ferrari 250 GTO
items.blurb: The most valuable car in the world, and the least useful data point on this page.
items.source: Public auction results — Bonhams 2014 ($38.1M), RM Sotheby's 2018 ($48.4M), Sotheby's 2023 ($51.7M)
items.caveat: A handful of sales of non-identical cars over twenty years. The CAGR is arithmetically true and practically meaningless — n is effectively three.

items.name: Porsche 911 Carrera
items.blurb: The last air-cooled 911. The most attainable car here, and it still tripled.
items.source: Auction results and market guides
items.caveat: Softened after 2023 along with most of the air-cooled market.

items.name: Lamborghini Countach
items.blurb: The other bedroom-wall poster.
items.source: Auction results and market guides
items.caveat: Early LP400s only; later QV and Anniversary cars are worth a fraction of this.

items.name: Cartier Love Bracelet
items.blurb: The default luxury gift, and partly a bet on the gold price.
items.source: Published US retail prices
items.caveat: Cartier reprices this with gold, so some of the rise is bullion rather than brand.

items.name: Van Cleef Vintage Alhambra
items.blurb: The other default, and a steeper climb than the Cartier.
items.source: Published US retail prices
items.caveat: Stone variants (onyx, mother-of-pearl, malachite) price differently; plain yellow gold is assumed.

items.name: Rolex Daytona 'Paul Newman'
items.blurb: The exotic-dial Daytona. Unsellable in the 1980s, the most wanted watch on earth by the 2010s.
items.source: Auction results; Newman's own example sold for $17.8M in 2017
items.caveat: Dial authenticity decides most of the value and is contested on many examples. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Patek Philippe Nautilus 3700/1A
items.blurb: Genta's original steel Nautilus, the ancestor of the 5711.
items.source: Auction results and dealer asking prices
items.caveat: Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Audemars Piguet Royal Oak 5402
items.blurb: The first Royal Oak, and the watch that invented the luxury steel sports category.
items.source: Auction results and dealer asking prices
items.caveat: Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: McLaren F1
items.blurb: Arguably the best-performing physical asset of the last twenty years.
items.source: Public auction results, including $20.5M at Gooding in 2021
items.caveat: Running costs are extraordinary and excluded here; a scheduled service runs into six figures. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Porsche 911 Carrera RS 2.7
items.blurb: The most collectible air-cooled 911.
items.source: Auction results and marque price guides
items.caveat: Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Karuizawa single cask
items.blurb: A closed Japanese distillery whose entire remaining stock was bought and released as single casks.
items.source: Auction hammer prices across the Bonhams Hong Kong and Whisky.Auction sales
items.caveat: A genuinely fixed supply from a distillery that shut in 2000. That is not repeatable by design. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: The Macallan 1926
items.blurb: The most valuable bottle of whisky in the world.
items.source: Public auction results — Bonhams 2018, Sotheby's 2019 and 2023 (£2.187M)
items.caveat: Forty bottles exist. A handful of sales over sixteen years; the rate is arithmetically true and practically meaningless. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Hermès Birkin 30 Himalaya
items.blurb: The graduated-grey crocodile Birkin, produced in tiny numbers and never openly offered.
items.source: Resale-platform and auction prices; the diamond-hardware version passed $380,000 at Christie's
items.caveat: Plain palladium hardware assumed. Very few public transactions. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Roland TR-808
items.blurb: A commercial failure in its day; the backbone of hip-hop and techno since.
items.source: Completed sales on the used-gear market
items.caveat: Condition and servicing swing this widely, and reissues have capped the top end. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Gibson Les Paul Standard 1959
items.blurb: The most mythologised electric guitar ever made. Roughly 640 were built.
items.source: Dealer asking prices and auction results
items.caveat: Included as a control: the most famous collectible guitar in the world, and it still loses to the index. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: F.P. Journe Chronomètre Bleu
items.blurb: An independent watchmaker's sleeper that became a status object.
items.source: Secondary-market asking prices and auction results
items.caveat: Another control: a famous multi-bagger that still trails the index once you measure from its own start. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.

items.name: Ferrari 250 GTO (private sales)
items.blurb: The private-sale record, as distinct from the auction record already in this database.
items.source: Widely reported private sales, including a reported $70M in 2018
items.caveat: Private sale figures are reported, not verified, and each car is unique. Survivorship bias in its purest form: this is on the list BECAUSE it won. For every one of these there are thousands of near-identical objects that did not, and no way to know in advance which was which.
